title: Low-tail-latency lab with Acme AI - p95 p99 streaming vs batch
summary: Deep dive focused on end-to-end tail latency (p95/p99) for Acme's inference workload. Covered streaming vs non-streaming, network hops (edge -> control plane -> private VPC), KV cache behavior for prefix reuse, batching windows and dynamic batching, quantization impacts on latency and quality, and measurable mitigations (local regional edge, tcp/keepalive, chunking). Agreed to run a live p99 streaming benchmark + warm-cold cache matrix; Redwood to share benchmark sheet and kernel/quant profiles.
topics: network topology and extra hops in VPC/private deployments
KV cache vs prefix caching behavior
dynamic batching windows and batching latency tradeoffs
quantization profiles impact on per-token latency
warm vs cold KV cache and cache priming strategies
action_items: Alex Nguyen | Share benchmark spreadsheet with columns: region, streaming_enabled, batch_size, p50/p95/p99, qps | Due: 2025-03-17
Samir Patel | Run streaming p99 load test against Acme test VPC (two regions) and capture tcp/traceroute hops | Due: 2025-03-19
Jordan Lee | Provide representative prompt set and 3k sample traces (cold, warm) | Due: 2025-03-16
Priya Malhotra | Open firewall 443 from Redwood test IPs to staging VPC; share bastion details | Due: 2025-03-14
next_steps: Schedule 2-hour hands-on benchmark run Thursday next week (Alex + Samir + Acme platform)
Redwood to attach quantization profiles (int8, fp16) and expected per-token latency delta in benchmark sheet
Customer to confirm SSO/role for logs access and provide initial SAML metadata if needed
Agree on p99 SLO target (initial ask: 250ms for streaming short sequences)
transcript:
[00:00] Alex (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
[00:07] Jordan (Acme): Jordan here, Priya, Ethan and Marta on.
[00:12] Samir (SE): Samir from Redwood, I'll drive the perf bits. Hi all.
[00:16] Marta (Product): Hi.
[00:20] Alex: Great. The purpose today is to dig into tail latency — p95 and p99 — and understand where your current hotspots are, especially given your expectation of sub-300ms p99 for short chat messages.
[00:34] Jordan: Yep, that's the ask. We've seen spikes. Sometimes p99 goes to 900ms even for 2-3 token turn.
[00:42] Samir: Ok, first, what does your current topology look like? Are you on our Private VPC or using Hosted?
[00:49] Priya: We're on Redwood Private deployed into our AWS account, VPC peering to some internal infra. We route via an internal NLB and then to our bastion then to the model hosts.
[00:58] Samir: That path has a few extra hops — NLB health checks, TLS termination, sometimes an internal proxy — each adds tail risk. If there's a cold KV cache miss, we add model KV lookups and that can amplify p99.
[01:15] Ethan: Explanation: in our deployment we also have an egress inspection layer for compliance. Could that be adding 100-200ms?
[01:22] Samir: Potentially. Middleboxes are common culprits. We'll want traceroutes during the benchmark. Also check keepalive settings and TLS session reuse.
[01:30] Alex: Important lens: streaming vs non-streaming. Streaming uses a HTTP/2 or gRPC chunked stream and can shave perceived latency because tokens are piped as soon as ready. But for p99 you need to measure end-to-end: network buffering, proxy timeouts, and client-side reassembly.
[01:48] Jordan: We're on HTTP/2 streaming for the chat UI.
[01:52] Samir: Good. But check the client library's flow control windows. If the browser's consumer is slower, server side may buffer and introduce spikes.
[02:02] Priya: Quick question: we saw better p95 but p99 still bad when traffic spikes. Is that KV cache related?
[02:09] Samir: Likely. Two common patterns: prefix reuse (many sessions share a few prompt prefixes) — that's great for KV/ prefix caching — or completely unique prompts, which cause cache churn. When cache cold, you'll see an extra 20-100ms for KV lookups and potentially 150-300ms if model has to recompute from scratch depending on seq len.
[02:28] Maria (SE): Also quantization matters. A well-tuned int8 kernel on Ampere or H100 might reduce token compute time by 25-40%, but quantization can increase the tail if dequant/dequant steps are not fused in kernel. Some older kernels do more memcpy which shows up at p99.
[02:47] Jordan: We're on older stable quant profile from last year. Can switching help p99?
[02:52] Samir: Sometimes yes — but test. We should run the p99 matrix with fp16, int8 fused, and int8 naive. We'll include that in the sheet.
[03:01] Alex: Let's talk measurement methodology. For p95/p99, run steady-state at target QPS for 10-15 minutes and collect distributions. Then run spike tests (triples of QPS) and cold-start windows. Also separate streaming vs non-streaming tests: streaming latency measured as time-to-first-token and time-to-last-token.
[03:22] Jordan: Good point about TTF token. Our UI cares mostly about time-to-first-token for UX.
[03:29] Samir: Exactly. For little turns, TTF dominates. For long completions p99 of end-to-end is different.
[03:37] Ethan: You mentioned batching — we use dynamic batching in prod. How does batch scheduling affect tail?
[03:42] Samir: Batch windows are a tradeoff. If you wait up to 10ms for a batch, p50 improves but p99 can get worse if windows expand under load. Redwood's continuous batching attempts to minimize queue delay using adaptive thresholds, but the policy matters. For low-latency customers we set aggressive max-wait 3-5ms and max-batch 8. That keeps p99 tighter at the cost of throughput.
[04:05] Priya: Is there an easy knob on Redwood to limit batch window?
[04:09] Alex: Yes, in the model route config you can set max_batch_wait_ms and dynamic thresholds. We'll show example configs.
[04:16] Maria: Also note that batching interacts with quant kernels: large batches may trigger different kernel paths or cause memory pressure and kernel-switching overheads that only show up at the tail. We'll capture kernel traces.
[04:30] Jordan: Network: you mentioned TCP settings — what are the key ones?
[04:33] Samir: TCP keepalive, TCP_NODELAY (to avoid Nagle for small writes), OS receive buffer sizes, and TLS session reuse. Also consider HTTP/2 stream concurrency; if proxy serializes streams you'll see head-of-line blocking. Measure with h2load and tcpdump during the run.
[04:51] Alex: Another source: control-plane calls for routing/fallbacks. If policy triggers a fallback model (e.g., to a quantized cheaper variant) that routing can add 50-200ms depending on lookup latency; local cached routing table avoids that. On Private, make sure the control-plane proxies are regional.
[05:09] Priya: About KV cache priming — can we prewarm?
[05:12] Samir: Yes. We can prime popular prefixes into the KV store and pin in the model process to avoid cold misses. We'll do a warm vs cold matrix in the benchmark.
[05:21] Jordan: For instrumentation we use our own jaeger traces; can Redwood inject spans?
[05:25] Alex: We can emit spans and propagate trace context. We'll show an example. Also Console has token-level latency breakdowns.
[05:33] Marta: Any gotchas in VPC/on-prem that are special for tail latency?
[05:36] Samir: On-prem often has variable NIC drivers and missing TAS offloads; some setups disable GRO/GSO which increases CPU overhead and latency jitter. Also multi-tenant networks with oversubscription cause bursts. If you're in a colo, ensure NIC queue limits and driver offloads are tuned.
[05:53] Ethan: Kernel selection — you mentioned it before — how does that affect p99?
[05:57] Maria: The runtime will pick kernels based on seq len and batch size. If an edge case triggers a less-optimized kernel (e.g., long context + single batch), that kernel might be single-threaded and slow. We log kernel switches; during the test we'll capture NVTX traces.
[06:13] Samir: Another phenomenon: memory swapping. If GPU memory peaks and the OS triggers host-side pinning or paged allocations, p99 spikes massively. Monitor GPU oom events. We'll recommend headroom: keep 10-15% free VRAM for peaks.
[06:27] Jordan: Any quick wins?
[06:29] Samir: Yes. 1) Reduce batch max-wait to 3ms for chat flows. 2) Ensure HTTP/2 upstream with keepalive and disable proxy buffering. 3) Prewarm KV cache for hot prefixes. 4) Use fused int8 kernels if available. 5) Regionalize control-plane and avoid cross-region routing.
[06:48] Alex: Let's look at a concrete scenario Jordan sent: 20RPS with 3-token completions, spikes to 80RPS for 30 seconds. What do we expect p99 changes?
[06:59] Samir: If batch windows are 10ms and you get a spike, you'd see queuing plus kernel switching; p99 could multiply by 2-3x. With max-wait 3ms and aggressive autoscale with burst pools it'll be contained. Dedicated pools avoid noisy neighbor effects.
[07:18] Priya: Autoscale ramp time is a concern — is there warm standby?
[07:22] Alex: We support burst capacity and warm standby nodes for Dedicated to absorb short spikes. For Private you can pre-provision smaller pool and a fast warm-up script. We'll help tune that.
[07:33] Jordan: For the benchmark, can you simulate our egress inspection? That seemed to correlate with spikes.
[07:38] Samir: Yes, we can run tests through a simulated proxy that adds deterministic delay and jitter to observe impact on p99. We'll also run tests with the proxy bypassed.
[07:49] Ethan: What about streaming vs polling? Our UI sometimes switches to long-poll for mobile.
[07:54] Maria: Polling adds a full request/response cycle overhead; streaming generally wins for perceived latency if implemented right. But mobile networks with intermittency may need retries; that complicates p99 measurement. We'll include mobile network emulation in the test plan.
[08:12] Jordan: Any options for reducing tail caused by TLS handshake?
[08:16] Samir: Keep TLS sessions warm, use session tickets, and prefer TLS 1.3 with 0-RTT where appropriate. For mTLS in Private, pre-established connections or connection pooling can reduce handshake risk.
[08:28] Priya: Ok, let's define the test matrix now.
[08:31] Alex: Matrix rows: streaming on/off, quant FP16/int8-fused, batch max-wait 3/10ms, cold/warm, regional vs cross-region, proxy on/off. Each test run 10 minutes steady-state at 1x and 3x traffic. We'll capture p50/p95/p99 and ttf-first-token.
[08:54] Jordan: Sounds good.
[08:56] Samir: One more deep detail: tail at the model level often correlates with garbage collection on managing processes (Python GC, allocator fragmentation). We prefer a thin C++ runtime worker to reduce host jank. If you're on older manager images, GC pauses show as 50-200ms spikes. We'll verify process metrics.
[09:15] Marta: Who will run the smoke run?
[09:18] Alex: Samir will run initial load from Redwood test infra against your staging VPC. Jordan/Priya will open access. Then we'll do a joint run from your side to replicate with your network path.
[09:29] Priya: We'll open the rules and share bastion.
[09:32] Jordan: Anything else?
[09:34] Samir: We'll attach kernel NVTX, jaeger spans, and per-token breakdown in the sheet. Expect to see whether p99 is dominated by network, queuing, or kernel tail.
[09:44] Alex: Quick recap and actions.
[09:47] Jordan: Thanks, this was useful.
[09:50] Alex: Cool. We'll follow up with the benchmark link and schedule.
[09:53] Marta: Thanks all.
[10:00] [call ends]
